stops.name: Chinon, questioned before the cardinals, the absolution
stops.campa: In the great fortress on the Vienne, three cardinals sent by Clement V examine the Order's leaders. On the twentieth of August Molay is brought last before them. The parchment records his confession and, over the spitting, the strange half-refusal remembered from his reception: that when bidden to spit on the cross he chose to spit beside it, fearing to defile the wood. Having abjured heresy and sworn upon the Gospel, he is absolved of excommunication and restored to the Church's communion. Between Pope and King the Grand Master is a coin passed back and forth, absolved in one court and doomed in another.
stops.quote: And since he feared the receptor would draw back his hand and some spittle fall upon the cross, he did not spit on the hand, but spat beside the cross.
stops.quote_source: The Chinon Parchment (record of the interrogation of Jacques de Molay, August 1308)

stops.name: Paris, before the Papal Commission, the retraction
stops.campa: When the Papal Commission opens in Paris, Molay stands before it and takes back all he confessed. He will not acknowledge the crimes laid on his Order; he asks only to defend it, though he is no clerk and pleads his own poverty of learning against the trained doctors ranged against him. But the King has moved first and hard: in May of 1310, on the strength of the forced confessions, four and fifty Templars who dared retract are burned in a single day outside Paris. The lesson is not lost. The Grand Master falls silent, his defence choked in the smoke of his own brethren.
stops.quote: I am not learned enough to defend the Order as it deserves; I ask only to be heard, for the Order is pure and holy.
stops.quote_source: Reported testimony of Molay before the Papal Commission, Paris, November 1309 (paraphrase from the proceedings)

stops.name: Vienne, the Order suppressed, Vox in excelso
stops.campa: At the Council of Vienne, with Philip come in person to press the churchmen, Clement V dissolves the Order of the Temple: not by verdict of guilt, which the evidence will not bear, but by decree, for the scandal and infamy now clinging to its name. The bull Vox in excelso, 'A voice from on high,' ends two hundred years of the Poor Knights of Christ at a stroke of the pen. Their lands are given to the Hospital; their leaders wait still in prison, their fate reserved to the Pope. Molay, uncondemned and unfreed, endures in the dark of his cell.
stops.quote: Vox in excelso audita est — A voice was heard from on high, of lamentation and bitter weeping.
stops.quote_source: Opening of the bull Vox in excelso, Clement V, 22 March 1312

stops.name: Paris, the years in the dungeon
stops.campa: The Order is dead; its Grand Master is not. Uncondemned and unfreed, Molay lies year upon year in prison while the great men of the world settle the bones of the Temple: its lands to the Hospital, its treasure to the crown, its guilt or innocence to the reserved judgement of the Pope. He is near seventy now, the old soldier of Acre and Ruad, forgotten in the dark between the courts. He waits, an inconvenient survivor, until at last the King and the cardinals remember there is still a sentence to pronounce upon the last Master of the Temple.

stops.name: Paris, the scaffold before Notre-Dame, the last recantation
stops.campa: Seven years in the dungeon, and on the eighteenth of March the cardinals mount a scaffold before Notre-Dame to pronounce the Grand Master and Geoffroi de Charney to perpetual imprisonment on their old confessions. Then, before the whole city, Molay and Charney rise and cry out that they are guilty of one thing only: of having betrayed their holy Order by confessing to lies to save their lives, under torture, to please the King. The Temple, they proclaim, is innocent and its rule pure. The prelates recoil; the King, hearing of it, orders them burned the same day as relapsed heretics.
stops.quote: We are not guilty of the crimes charged against us; but we are guilty of basely betraying our Order to save our lives. The Order is pure, it is holy; the accusations are lies.
stops.quote_source: Continuator of William of Nangis, Chronicle, on 18 March 1314

stops.name: Île aux Juifs, the fire, and the summons from the flames
stops.campa: At evening a pyre is raised on the little Île aux Juifs in the Seine, below Notre-Dame between the royal gardens and the city. Molay asks that his hands be freed to pray and his face turned toward the church of the Virgin, of whom Christ was born; it is granted. The slow fire takes him, and men marvel that he dies with such stillness. From the flames the Grand Master calls his judges to God's tribunal: within the year Pope Clement and King Philip shall answer there. Clement dies within the month; Philip before the year is out. The Capetian line withers: les rois maudits, the accursed kings.
stops.quote: God knows who is in the wrong and has sinned; misfortune will soon fall on those who have wrongly condemned us. God will avenge our death. I beseech you, turn my face toward the Virgin Mary, of whom our Lord Christ was born.
stops.quote_source: Geoffroi de Paris, Chronique métrique, eyewitness of the burning, 18 March 1314
